summary.text: A female infant was born by emergency caesarean section for fetal distress at 39 weeks, after fetal dysrhythmia was diagnosed at 33 weeks of gestation. Fetal echocardiography showed couplets of premature ventricular beats; decreased contractile function and pericardial effusion led to transplacental sotalol, after which the intrauterine course was favorable with sinus rhythm and normalized ventricular function. She weighed 3370 g and was hemodynamically stable at birth.

The ECG immediately after birth showed sinus rhythm and a QTc of 380 ms, with normal first echocardiography. On the third day after birth a 24-h ECG showed recurrent repetitive monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. She was moved to the NICU, propranolol did not restore sinus rhythm, and amiodarone gave initially partial control. SARS-CoV infection was confirmed by rRT-PCR in infant and mother on the fifth day after delivery.

Workup for suspected myocardial injury found elevated troponin I and D-dimer, no other bacterial or viral infection, and a normal chest radiograph. Serial studies showed rising troponin I, D-dimer and ferritin, persistent pericardial effusion, progressive left coronary dilation and, on the twelfth day of COVID infection, LV systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction 30%. A possible inflammatory myocardial injury associated with COVID infection was considered.

Treatment included intravenous immunoglobulin, low-molecular-weight heparin, intravenous dexamethasone, an increased amiodarone dose, furosemide, spironolactone and levosimendan; antiplatelet therapy was described as required for coronary dilation. Evolution was favorable, with normalized TnI, NT-proBNP and D-dimer after 3 weeks of treatment and sinus rhythm on repeated 24-h ECG. She was discharged with LV systolic function recovery on oral heart failure therapy with close follow-up.
